chapter: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
title: Dizzy as a true original; jamming with Dizzy and Ben Webster
summary: Dizzy was different from other Eldridge imitators; they jammed in Collins's hotel room and at the Grampion Hotel with Ben Webster.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

Yeah, well you see Roy and Dizzy knew eachother. Well, they knew eachother, they'd played before I ever went to New York, before Roy came to Chicago with Fletcher Henderson. So I didn't know anything about Dizzy, you know. And all I knew that all the trumpet players tried to play like Roy. Everybody but Dizzy.
Dizzy said he did and went on from (inaudible).

Well, yeah, yeah, possibly. But when I got to New York the scene had changed, as far as Dizzy is concerned, and Roy. But it was always different. He was a true individual musically, you know, he had his own ideas. And we used to jam all the time. He'd come up to my hotel room and we would just play and exchange ideas, and then we used to go to another hotel called the Grampion. Now, who's living there? Ben Webster. And the three of us would play, we'd just sit there all day and just play, and exchange ideas. And I always thought Ben was -- what can I say, exquisite. He's beauty, he's just sheer beauty, you know.
So I really got to know Dizzy, musically and
otherwise. And as I say he was -- I always admired him because he was -- you had to put him over there. He was different. But any way, let me take a breather. Okay? [pause in tape]
